newsitem.title: GERMANY: U.S. expresses concern over Japan's shaky finances.
newsitem.headline: U.S. expresses concern over Japan's shaky finances.

text.p: The United States voiced concern on Saturday over Japan's fragile economy and banking system and said it would keep close watch on developments there for potential fallout on the rest of the world.

In what for him were unusually blunt remarks, U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin used a news conference after a meeting of the Group of Seven (G7) industrial nations to focus on economic troubles besetting Japan.
"They clearly have difficult issues to deal with," he said, adding "these concerns merit a fair bit of attention going forward.'
After surging in the early part of last year, Japan's economy has taken a turn for the worse, raising the spectre that it could even slip back into recession.

Such concerns have sent Japanese equity markets into a tailspin in recent weeks, prompting worries that the already shaky banking system might see a series of defaults, which could hurt the world economy.
No where is the concern greater than in the United States, which still has a large trade deficit with Japan and benefits from Japanese investment.
One scenario posited by experts has a run on the Japanese banking system leading to a massive repatriation of capital out of the United States and back to Tokyo.
Japan is the largest foreign holder of U.S. government debt.
Japanese Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka reassured Rubin on Saturday that Japan would continue to pursue economic policies to promote strong domestic demand.
Japanese officials say their economy is still on an upward path and argue that their stock market has taken an overly gloomy view of the country's prospects.
But U.S. officials are worried Japanese plans for a sharp tightening of budget policy, including a big increase in consumption taxes, could cast a pall over the economy.
"This is a committment (from Japan) we, in the United States, take very seriously," said a senior Treasury official who declined to be named.
"It is a real possibility this would require further action on the part of Japan," he added.
He said the United States was focused on Japan because of the shaky banking system and fears about a renewed rise in the country's trade surplus.
"The Japan issue has the financial element and also has concerns about the re-emergence of a large global surplus," the official said.
